en: From those who devoured lives in combat,
He would turn the mouth of a swift steed
With a camel’s forelock and a low mane.
Gathering many such men,
My lion uncle, fierce with wrath—
Men mighty and strong,
My heroic uncle Semetey—
Would test their strength.
In the marshlands of broad Talas,
My dear uncle, my lion uncle,
While the great Kyrgyz people lived in peace,
We dwelt in broad Talas.
When one day my destined fate
Would not let me rest,
When my trouser legs
Could scarcely contain me,
Finding no cliff from which to fly to my death,
No enemy against whom to die fighting,
No mountain high enough to cross,
No bullet with which to shoot,
And no road along which to ride,
When he charged, he tore lives apart;
He also had such ferocity
That ten ranks of men could not sate him.
Yet the unreformed Choro
Also had his clumsiness.
Canopy of the shining river,
Hero of humankind,
From the broad plain where cries rang out,
From the broad ravine where no bird flew—
So spoke the hero Seytek,
And set ninety mattocks
Side by side in rows.
“You were a great lord and a lion,
You were such a gray-wolf hero!
Have your flourishing days
Passed away, my princely uncle?
After suffering days of grief and misery,
Meeting the strength of the wrathful,
And enduring so many ordeals,
Has your body weakened and your strength departed,
Has all your power grown weary and spent?
Has it left you, my princely uncle?
If you still have power and are a hero,
Summon your ancient strength.
The foe you must grapple with is Kanchoro,
Like the shoulder of a dark rocky mountain;
The hero you must contend with is Kyyaz,
Like tempered red iron.
Do not let it be said that Külchoro,
His strength gone, was killed by them.
Undertake this mighty ordeal,
My peerless and illustrious uncle,
And put your strength to the test.
If your vigor boils and your strength runs full,
If you are as you were at first,
Then wage battle.”
So spoke the hero Seytek:
“When Kanchoro turned treacherous
And drove your people from Keng-Kol,
We should have set eighty mattocks
Before that swaggering villain
And tested his strength;
Only afterward should that wretched soul
Have gone to fight the enemy.”
When he had spoken thus,
The hero Seytek, son of a champion,
To test his uncle’s power,
To measure him against Kyyaz, the hero’s son,
And send him against the foe,
To avenge his ancient wrong,
Caught and slaughtered forty barren mares
From among the horses,
And, to test Külchoro’s strength,
Set ninety stout mattocks
Together in a row.
Would Külchoro, favored by the spirits,
Shrink from the contest?
He tested his former strength.
The Choro, ready with the spear,
Still possessed his skill.
His name was known throughout the world,
And in Beijing his one name
Was inscribed in the chronicles.
His wrestling strength was extraordinary,
His heroism beyond measure;
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
A sturdy, powerfully built giant,
He raged like a tiger,
And none who fought him survived.
He charged like a wild boar,
And grappled like a snow leopard.
His stride was like a tiger’s,
And none who met him survived.
His sweeping coat measured eighty-four spans;
When he surged forward, he was crimson fire.
If you saw his appearance, it was thus:
A manifest calamity and disaster,
Terrible in majesty and mighty in venom,
A camel-built scourge
Who leveled all who wrestled him.
His entire body was strength;
He was renowned, a pillar,
A champion and a lion.
He was a dark mountain crowned with crags,
A towering, lofty peak,
A steel bullet against the enemy,
Among all mortal sons ever born,
An undying crimson ember.
Among all the sons of men,
No champion like him had ever lived.
He was truly a servant of God,
A valiant eagle of bloodthirsty Manas,
A mighty lion’s son.
Wearing a sword without a sheath,
He roamed the whole wide world,
Broke through dead ends and opened roads,
And struck in every direction.
Hardened and sated with blood,
Among all the people
He was famed as the leopard Choro.
He was an undying beacon-fire;
Among mortal humankind
No other wrought such devastation.
Since his gray-wolf lord had died,
He had suffered bitter torment.
His two hands were gouged,
He was flayed and brought to disgrace,
His days narrowed to a handbreadth,
And all he saw was bloody misery.
The boy had inflicted horrors upon him,
His joints had gone soft and trembled,
And yellow fluid had flooded them.
“How much strength has he left?” they wondered,
And the milling crowd pondered;
All the people stood like this.
The lion Choro, son of Almambet,
The hero Choro, favored by the spirits,
Had wearied horses while seeing distant lands,
And wearied nations while seeing many peoples.
His heroism was beyond measure—
“Now take your vengeance thus!”
So spoke the hero Seytek.
The descendant of swift-footed lions
Turned his swift steed’s head,
And tested the strength
Of his mighty uncle Choro.
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Blazed like a crimson ember;
None like him had existed since creation.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Both wrestler and lion,
No such hero comes from humankind.
Broad-breasted and wide-chested,
Handsome in form, with dark eyes,
The born champion Külchoro
Before Kyzylsart and Kara-Döö,
And many honored choros,
Set ninety mattocks
Together in a row.
Fat oozed from the hero’s thumb,
And blood came from his throat;
The bones of his arms bent,
His ribs warped apart,
And his joint bones crackled.
His broad front teeth, like a gate,
Teeth unlike those of common men,
Cracked each time he clenched them.
For the poor man favored by the spirits,
Ninety formidable mattocks
Had been set out in a row.
They witnessed the heroism
Of the poor man favored by the spirits;
The gathered people watched and proclaimed it,
Marveling at my champion.
The people cried out in an uproar,
Their clamor splitting the sky;
The great multitude acclaimed him,
And all the people marveled
At the renowned gray-wolf champion.
All his remaining strength was ready
To unleash slaughter without looking back.
If his old vigor returned to his limbs,
He would avenge the gray wolf’s death.
They told Choro, “Shoot through
The ninety mattocks in a row,”
And thus put his courage to the test.
To shoot through those mattocks,
Külchoro, favored by the spirits,
Would measure what strength he had.
If powerless, he would die of shame
Before death itself could come;
If he had the strength, he meant
To unleash some great calamity;
If this poor man had no strength,
He would surrender his fly-like soul.
He took the steel bow in his hand,
His heart aflame and his eyes blazing,
Biting his lip and grinding his teeth;
The poor defender of the people
Stood with both eyes blazing.
He readied himself like a hawk,
And found wisdom in his courage;
The troubled poor hero
Found keen strength within his body
And strung the mighty bow.
He gathered his strength in his mind,
Mustered his courage throughout his body,
Prepared to draw the bow,
And prayed to the Creator.
Every watcher’s attention was seized;
His lion-like aspect appeared.
His form was like a massive boulder,
And your rugged eagle seemed
Ready to devour anyone who crossed him.
If the gray-wolf servant surveyed the world,
He seemed capable of conquering it;
For ages beyond the Jediger,
His cry seemed fit to unleash slaughter.
Whoever came within his reach
He seemed able to cleave and cast down.
Such was his wrestling might.
Wide-mouthed and cliff-browed—
Behold and ponder his gray-wolf courage.
He broke through passes and opened roads,
And, heedless of his own destruction,
Attacked an army six hundred thousand strong.
The hero Choro, pillar of the people,
Was fed carved horse-rib meat and fat,
And given plentiful food.
The orphan-raised hero Seytek
Had special delicacies prepared:
Fat lambs and choice heads,
And thick white broth boiled;
He had him crunch sugar white as snow
And gulp liquor from a bowl.
“I have tended my uncle well,” he said,
“For I know he is a lion.
If my uncle remains alive,
He will yet prove useful.”
So the people had said
Of my dear gray-wolf uncle:
“There is none like him in the world,”
As those who had seen him from afar knew,
Amid sky-splitting turmoil
And in single combat.
If he truly was a pillar,
The chieftain’s surviving legacy,
If he truly was a lion,
His courage must now have sharpened and filled him;
The time must have come for him
To clash with Kyyaz, son of Bagysh.
To put his strength to the test—
If his vigor had matured against the Jediger
Who filled the Seven Valleys—
To take revenge upon Kyyaz,
